new_statements.quote: p. 42: "The first type of polysyllabic words is called sequisyllabic. As found in other Mon-Khmer languages, sequisyllabic words have a stressed main syllable, which is preceded by an unstressed and phonological reduced minor syllable (Matisoff, 1973). The minor syllable can either be presyllable CV, as in (2a-b), or presyllabic nasal, as in (2c-d). Note that in Dara-ang the major stressed syllable of sequisyllabic words can be preceded by two presyllables CVCV, as in (2e-f)." p. 74: "The first type of polysyllabic word in the Da-ang Palaung dialect of Kalaw city is a sequisyllabic word, which has a stressed main syllable that is preceded by an unstressed and phonological reduced minor syllable."
new_statements.citation: Buakaw, Supakit. 2012. A phonological study of Palaung dialects spoken in Thailand and Myanmar, with focuses on vowels and final nasals. PhD dissertation, Mahidol University.
new_statements.locator: Section 4.1.2 'Polysyllabic words', p. 42 (PDF page 58), Dara-ang of No-Lae; the same statement for Da-ang of Kalaw in section 5.1.2, p. 74 (PDF page 90)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: I re-extracted PDF pages 58 and 90 with extracted text and decoded the +29 font shift myself: page 58 (running head 'Supakit Buakaw / Dara-ang Phonology / 42', section 4.1.2 'Polysyllabic words') reads 'The first type of polysyllabic words is called sequisyllabic. As found in other Mon-Khmer languages, sequisyllabic words have a stressed main syllable, which is preceded by an unstressed and phonological reduced minor syllable (Matisoff, 1973). The minor syllable can either be presyllable CV, as in (2a-b), or presyllabic nasal, as in (2c-d). Note that in Dara-ang the major stressed syllable of sequisyllabic words can be preceded by two presyllables CVCV, as in (2e-f).' Page 90 (running head…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for ruch1235, so this is the first prose statement of stress placement for the language. It matches the pattern implicit in the earlier reading's transcriptions (Buakaw 2014, 2009: stress marked on the major syllable) and Buakaw, Rattanapitak & Deepadung 2018 on Katiang Palaung ('presyllable is an unstressed syllable').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables, sesquisyllables (one or two unstressed, phonologically reduced minor syllables + one major syllable) or compounds. In a sesquisyllabic word the stress falls on the major syllable, which is always the last syllable; the presyllable(s) or presyllabic nasal preceding it are unstressed. The statement is made for both dialects studied (Dara-ang, No-Lae, Thailand; Da-ang, Kalaw, Myanmar). Nothing is said about stress in compounds (which are treated as sequences of two words) or about tone; vowel length is phonemic and is the thesis's main topic.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The thesis explicitly allows a major stressed syllable to be preceded by two presyllables (CVCV), so stress is not simply 'second syllable' but 'the final/major syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Buakaw 2012 describes two varieties, both Pale/Silver Palaung [pce] = Ruching Palaung: Dara-ang of No-Lae village, Fang district, Chiang Mai (Thailand) and Da-ang of Nyaung Gone village, Kalaw, southern Shan State (Myanmar); the stress statement is made for each. Per Buakaw (p. 16), Janzen 1978's 'Pale' or 'Di-ang' is the Kalaw Da-ang variety; Kasisopa 2003 describes the No-Lae Dara-ang variety.

Phonologically, presyllable is an unstressed syllable the vowel of which is limited to low central vowel /a/'; p.6: 'The minor syllable of Katiang is an unstressed syllable, namely a presyllable'. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No prose statement on stress. Da-ang (Kalaw) is the Pale/Silver Palaung variety (pce). Phonetic transcriptions of sesquisyllabic words consistently place primary stress on the major (final) syllable: [saˈpən] 'lips', [saˈnaʔ] 'tender', [sɔˈdaːʔ] 'hot' (ex. 1, p.6); [kaˈtɛː] 'center', [kaˈpɔː] 'gourd', [ʔaˈsei] 'who', [maˈnou] 'teach' (ex. 2-3, p.7); uses the term 'major open syllables' (p.7).
